properties.project_name: Biochar Project-1 by WeAct
properties.methodology: VM0044 Methodology for Biochar Utilization in Soil and Non-Soil Applications
properties.verra_project_name_current: Biochar Project-1 by WeAct
properties.verra_project_description: This project activity is a voluntary initiative by WeAct Pty Ltd in the Sangareddy district, in the state of Telangana in India. WeAct is a carbon asset management and carbon financing entity from Australia who deals in such GHG projects globally to address the concerns of climate change and ensures long term sustainability. The project activity uses Low technology production facilities to produce Biochar from biomass wastes in the project region. The project includes mainly soil-pit methods and box-kiln method which are two common low-tech approaches that can serve as a starting point for small-scale production, experimentation, and community-level initiatives. Under the facilities, the biomass undergoes pyrolysis process. The project activity mainly targets to include “Cotton Stalk” as a single type of waste biomass used as feedstock to produce biochar and the resulting biochar to be utilized for soil application. In the absence of the project activity, the cotton wastes would have been mainly combusted without any utilization for purposes and not utilized for producing biochar for either soil or non-soil application. The project activity is expected to generate an annual average of 22,376 tCO2e emission reductions which is estimated based on a projected generation of biochar from cotton stalks as feedstock during each harvesting season in each year. The project contributes to sustainable development by promoting various aspects including (but not limited to) environmental conservation, resource efficiency, rural development, climate change mitigation, and the transition towards a circular economy. It aligns agricultural practices with the principles of sustainable development, fostering a more resilient and equitable agricultural sector.

properties.verra_project_description: Gauthans are village-based cow-dung processing premises that have emerged as multi-activity centres supporting vermicomposting production and livelihood-based activities for Self-help groups in the Chhattisgarh state of India. The avoidance of methane emissions is achieved with treatments of aerobic composting with the help of Worms, which replaces the baseline scenario where the manure would undergo anaerobic decomposition conditions. In this project, the collected cattle manure is utilised through a composting process with the help of Worms. Worms convert the cattle manure aerobically into vermicompost used for application to lands.  Without this project, the farms in project areas remain conditions of uncovered anaerobic lagoons that may bring a larger amount of GHG emissions sent to the atmosphere. Utilising cattle manure for vermicompost preparation has the primary benefit of reduced methane emission along with secondary benefit of replacing fertilisers in farm inputs which contribute for emission reduction. During the implementation of the project, it is estimated that about 117,000 tons of dairy manure would be treated and composted, with 30,000tons of organic fertiliser generated per year. Besides, the GHG emissions are expected to reduce 59918 tCO2e per year and 419424 tCO2e in a 7-year crediting period.

properties.verra_project_description: The Regeneration Meghalaya Project is a grouped project under ARR (Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation) category that aims to increase tree cover through planting a majority of indigenous trees that are suited to local conditions of the bioregion. The project is located in the Khasi, Ri Bhoi Jaintia and Garo Hills regions, in the Northeastern state of Meghalaya, India. Regeneration Meghalaya will plant trees across up to 30,000 ha of wasteland. The project aims to plant up to 40 - 64 million trees sequestering up to 23 Million tonnes of CO2e in Meghalaya. In addition, the project aims to reach a significant number of beneficiaries over a period of 35 years. The GHG (greenhouse gas) removals in the project would be created by improving the land though planting new trees and plants in the eligible project areas. The project’s broader aims are to restore ecological integrity, reduce soil erosion, improve ecological functions, increase biodiversity and improve livelihoods. In this regard, the project will monitor and report on the co-benefits for climate adaptation, biodiversity and people through the climate, community and biodiversity standard (CCB). The project taps into and is led by indigenous knowledge custodians to accelerate landscape restoration and sustainably develop both tree-based and non-tree based products to create value chains and grow sustainable livelihoods. The project goals are aligned to the local needs and existing land use systems, farmer-led species selection that prioritise indigenous and naturalised species, and customised solutions to challenges identified by local stakeholders. The project area is home to the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo tribes, and the majority of the land is held under private / clan ownership, with some community control and management.

Together for Restoration presents Project Reignite, aimed at transforming agricultural waste into biochar for soil enrichment in India, with an initial cohort of 5,000 farmers in the state of Odisha. properties.methodology: AR-ACM0003 Afforestation and reforestation of lands except wetlands

properties.verra_primary_category: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_name_current: Tasar Forest Carbon Project
properties.verra_sectoral_scope_current: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_description: This Tasar Forest Carbon Project will promote tree-based wild silk production outside traditional forests by utilizing privately owned barren / fallow uplands of tribal farmers. The project will undertake wild silk (locally called Tasar) tree planting and promote sericulture-based livelihoods. Sericulture is a traditional livelihood, however lack of availability of host trees in natural forests constrains its expansion. Traditionally, the tribal communities in the targeted areas depend majorly on forests for their livelihoods and have a long history of wild silk production from natural forests – wild silk is second to agriculture as a source of livelihoods. However, production from the forests declined due to government regulation of forest access rights. Yet there are large areas in these regions that are severely degraded, fallow, etc. that would benefit from restoring their productive capacity and biodiversity through profitable tree planting investments. The project is implemented by Cognisphere Solutions Ltd. (CSL) with investment from Climate Partner Impact GmbH starting in 2022. The project will afforest 2,000 hectares of privately-owned wastelands with Tasar silk-host trees in the adjoining states of Jharkhand and West Bengal in India. The project implementation started from May 2022 and plantations were initiated in the season Jun to Oct 2022. It will involve the participation of ~3,000 households in 125 villages, grouped into two clusters broadly in Jharkhand, and West Bengal. People in the project areas are majorly tribals with limited options to escape poverty and deprivation. Tasar host trees such as Terminalia arjuna and T. tomentosa will form the core species, accompanied with a diversity of other indigenous tree species. The planted trees will be managed as long-term agroforestry systems –integrating crop production (intercropping), Tasar silk production and associated value chain development.

properties.verra_sectoral_scope_current: Energy industries (renewable/non-renewable sources),Waste handling and disposal
properties.verra_project_description: The project activity is a biogas-based electricity generation project. The project involves methane recovery through controlled anaerobic digestion of poultry waste and utilization of recovered biogas to produce electricity. The project involves installation of two centralized anaerobic bio-digesters having capacities of 1500m3/day each, at the existing two poultry firms of the project owner with a total capacity of 3000 m3/day and utilization of one number of 100 KVA and one number of 250 kVA capacity biogas based electrical engines for each biogas unit.   On an average each poultry farm produces about 18 MT of poultry manure per day with total of 36 MT from two poultry firms. The electricity generated from the project is utilized for the captive use in the poultry farms.  The project activity is being implemented in phased manner where the first 1500m3 biogas unit is installed in phase I and second 1500 m3 biogas unit is installed in phase II. The project is owned and operated by Sunmax Hatcheries Private Limited company. The project is located in DasarlaPalli Village in Siddipet district of Telangana State, India. Prior to the implementation of the project activity, the poultry manure waste utilized by the project activity is left to decay in open pits, tanks or anaerobic lagoons at the poultry farms, where the manure undergoes fermentation and release methane, that is emitted to the atmosphere directly without any methane recovery and destruction facility. For electricity component, prior to the implementation of the project activity, the electricity supply for the poultry farm was generated mainly from grid connected power plants.

properties.verra_sectoral_scope_current: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_description: Grow Indigo is implementing a regenerative agriculture-based carbon project in the extensive rice cultivation states of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Odisha, and Telangana in India. The project area is characterized by traditional and intensive cultivation practices within diverse ecological systems, which emit significant amounts of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The southern region, encompassing Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka, excels in irrigated rice farming and cultivation in deltaic and non-deltaic regions. At the same time, Chhattisgarh and Odisha specialize in rainfed upland and lowland rice cultivation. Intensive agriculture practices in the project area have threatened food security and contributed to increased GHG emissions. The Grow Indigo project aims to incentivise farmers for adopting regenerative agriculture practices, thereby achieving the mitigation of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and fostering positive environmental and economic outcomes. Regenerative agriculture is a holistic farming system that focuses on improving soil health, biodiversity, and water quality. It can help to reduce GHG emissions by sequestering carbon in the soil. These practices include improved fertilizer management, cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced tillage, improved water management, crop residue management, agroforestry, etc. The project will also help to build the capacity of farmers to adopt regenerative agriculture practices through training and technical support. The project aims to scale up to 4 million hectares within the project area over a 5-year period. During the 20-year crediting period, it is estimated that there will be an average annual reduction and removal of 5,326,066 tCO2e. This innovative project has the potential to make a significant contribution to sustainable agriculture and climate change mitigation in India.

This project is taking a bold step towards environmental sustainability in the Ganga basin region of India. Common agricultural practice in these areas includes conventional methods such as heavy use of synthetic fertilizers, intensive tillage, crop residue burning, and excessive water consumption for irrigation. These practices have led to soil depletion and accelerated greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, threatening the ecosystem of the Ganga basin. The transition to regenerative agriculture is vital to counteract soil degradation, fertility loss, water pollution, and natural resource depletion. This shift is crucial to maintain the ecosystem services of the Ganga basin. The potential impact of the VCS carbon project is immense. It promises to significantly reduce GHG emissions, improve soil health, and enhance biodiversity. Beyond environmental benefits, the project aims to uplift the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and enhance the resilience of the Ganga basin ecosystem in the face of climate change. Over a five-year period, the project aims to scale up to cover 4 million hectares within the Ganga basin region of the project area. The 20-year crediting period is expected to yield an average annual emission reduction and removal of 5,048,425 tCO2e. Grow Indigo's efforts in this project exemplify a proactive and holistic approach to tackle environmental challenges, offering a ray of hope for the Ganga basin and its residents.

properties.verra_project_description: The Panna Afforestation and Reforestation Project, is a grouped Afforestation, Reforestation and Revegetation (ARR) project, planting a diverse range of native tree species on community and private land in Madhya Pradesh, India in partnership with local implementation partners and local communities. The project targets a mix of large-scale afforestation and reforestation on areas of degraded community (Gram Panchayat) land and the plantation of economically beneficial trees in and around smallholder farmers’ fields. Over the next 6 years, the project will plant over 11 million trees, comprising a mix of approximately 19 different native species, selected in consultation with communities and farmers, on an expected 19,000 hectares. In addition to ARR activities, the project also involves the construction of water infrastructure facilities such as ponds, dams and community tanks to improve water availability, tree survival and local biodiversity. Water irrigation through borewells and solar pumps help to improve irrigation within the project area. The project also intends to support agricultural productivity gains and minimise amongst participating farmers through an extensive training program, focusing on concepts such as climate smart agriculture practises, zero tillage, and improved mulching. A multi-faceted project that goes beyond carbon sequestration, the Panna Project also supports local livelihoods, improves food and water availability, sustainably raises agricultural yields, and positively impacts biodiversity across the project area. Through a community fund approach, the community members will benefit from a share of the carbon revenue as well as a multi-million dollar upfront funding commitment to improve education, healthcare and other aspects of life in the region.

properties.verra_project_description: India's agricultural sector faces pressing environmental challenges, notably due to conventional waste disposal methods such as open field burning and unmanaged biomass decay. These practices contribute significantly to greenhouse gas emissions and broader environmental degradation. Addressing this, Together for Restoration (a program by SRCNatura Sure Pvt. Ltd.) introduces Project Terre Boost, an initiative aimed at transforming agricultural residues into biochar for soil enhancement across seven Indian states—Assam, Nagaland, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, and Jharkhand.  Project Terre Boost employs flame curtain pyrolysis technology in steel-shielded soil pits to convert agricultural waste into biochar. This biochar, mixed with manure and applied deep into the soil, promises a sustainable solution to waste management in agriculture. The project includes an initial cohort of 5,000 farmers (biochar producers). Environmental impacts of Project Terre Boost are substantial, with an estimated annual removal of 116,961 tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e), totalling 818,727 tCO2e over a seven-year crediting period. Moreover, the advantages of Project Terre Boost transcend environmental considerations, creating a dual advantage by significantly elevating the welfare of marginalised local farming communities.

properties.verra_project_description: Godhan Nyay Yojana is a scheme launched by the Government of Chhattisgarh in India to promote sustainable rural development by incentivising cattle owners to manage and use cow dung effectively. The scheme involves collecting cow dung from cattle owners and converting it into vermicompost, sold in the market through farmer cooperatives. The aim is to generate income for rural households promoting organic farming and reducing cow dung's environmental impact. Methane emissions from cattle dung primarily occur when it decomposes in anaerobic conditions, such as in traditional dung pits or open fields. These emissions are a significant contributor to greenhouse gases. The Godhan Nyay Yojana is designed to address this issue by incentivizing the collection and management of cow dung, which reduces methane emissions through vermicomposting.

properties.verra_project_description: The project is a strategic initiative targeting social, economic, and environmental concerns through the transition of farmers toward sustainable agricultural practices. Focused on the Central Plateau, Southern Plateau, and East Coast Plains region of India, it leverages existing relationships with smallholder farmers, historically reliant on conventional agricultural methods like frequent tillage and chemical fertilisers. The initiative introduces sustainable practices like Dry-Direct Seeded Rice (DSR), Wet-DSR, and Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) for paddy cultivation to combat methane emissions, along with zero tillage and cover cropping to increase carbon stock. Additionally, it introduces crop residue management, improved fertiliser practices, green manuring, and agroforestry to promote carbon sequestration and reduce synthetic inputs. The primary goal is to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions through regenerative agriculture and agroforestry, fostering sustainable land management. Anticipated benefits encompass improved soil quality, heightened biodiversity, decreased environmental degradation, and carbon sequestration. These positive outcomes aim to bolster the well-being of smallholder farmers by enhancing agricultural productivity and profitability.

properties.verra_project_description: The grouped project’s aim is to undertake agroforestry on fallow/ degraded lands of the individual smallholder farmers holding 0.2 to 1 ha of land in Jharkhand, India, through the establishment of horticultural trees yielding fruits, and timber based agroforestry model and by intercropping of seasonal crops in the farmers plot. The first instance consists of afforestation of 5000 hectare (ha) of fallow lands owned by local smallholder farmers that are lying unutilized for decades owing to various reasons such as lack of financial resources, migrant labor, etc. The project entails the planting of a variety of native species depending primarily on the soil types and local (market) demand, in consultation with the community members, for example, timber yielding trees comprising Teak (Tectona Grandis) and fruit yielding types including Mango (Mangifera Indica), Guava (Psidium guajava), Orange (Citrus Sinensis), among other species. To ensure the longevity and sustainability of the project, it will be managed by the local community. The activities under the project will contribute to multiple indicators for the Sustainable Development Goals such as No poverty (SDG 1), Zero Hunger (SDG 2), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Clean Water and Sanitation (SDG 6), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 9), Climate Action (SDG 13), Life on Land (SDG 15).  The overall goal of the project is to, through afforestation activities, recover and utilize fallow lands and to promote connectivity between ecosystems by providing pathways for wildlife, facilitating movement and genetic exchange between fragmented habitats. In addition the project is majorly focused on enhancing livelihoods of the local communities in the project area. Marginal farmers in Jharkhand suffer from low income due to low productivity due to existing issues such as less fertile land, less use of manure, greater dependence on monsoons, backward/ outdated and limited technology, and unproductive use of debt.

The project promotes and implements the plantation of Eucalyptus species with short rotations in privately owned lands of small and marginal farmers in the project area. Maharashtra (63.7% ) and Odisha (20.61% ) are among the largest contributors to the agricultural sector of the country, and are majorly dependent on rain-fed agriculture (around 75% - 80%  ) for sustenance making them vulnerable to the changing climatic conditions. Rise in temperature, unpredictable rainfall, soil erosion and increasing drought are among the major conditions that are affecting the productivity of the land leading to crop failure  . Urvara Krsi Private Limited (UKPL) has been promoting agroforestry with small & marginal farmers belonging to various tribal communities across the states of India. UKPL with its landscape approach is implementing plantations under models such as Block plantation, Wadi Model (NABARD), Bund Plantation etc. in agricultural areas, bunds, wasteland, community land, and barren land. They provides expert technical guidance to the farmers on the selection and maintenance of plantations and assists in creating market linkage for the sale of timber/pulp. This model not only helps in increasing the productivity of the land but also creates additional livelihood opportunities for the farmers. The project area is estimated to carry out plantation on 13,255 ha of land between 2021 to 2024. Over a crediting period of 29 years the project will generate gross removals or net removals of 12,63,577 tCO2e and 43,571 tCO2e/yr.

properties.project_name: CORE CARBON SOLAR POWER PROJECT
properties.methodology: AMS-I.F. Renewable electricity generation for captive use and mini-grid
properties.verra_project_name_current: CORE CARBON SOLAR POWER PROJECT
properties.verra_project_description: The proposed project activity involves the installation of rooftop and ground mounted solar panels for captive consumption. The surplus electricity if generated can be supplied to the grid and if there is deficit of energy, that can be consumed from grid through a net metering arrangement with the respective state electricity board. The Net Metering concept states that the customers are to be charged only for the net power that they consume from the electricity service provider that has accumulated over a specific period. In other terms if the installed renewable energy produces more electricity than the consumed then the producer would be paid or credited for the excess amount of electricity generation to the grid over the same period. The Net Metering helps the grid to supply in the peak hours to keep up with increase demand in peak hours. It has been observed that in the actual scenario, no surplus power is exported to the grid as the internal demand of the premises is very high and the status quo is expected to be maintained throughout the operation of the projects. Hence, none of the instances export greater than 50% of generated electricity to the grid, so the project eligibility in the VCS program is justified. The geographical location of the project is entire India. The project activity will displace electricity from an electricity distribution system that is or would have been supplied by at least one fossil fuel fired generating unit i.e., in the absence of the project activity, the users would have been supplied electricity from one or more sources listed below: (a) A national or a regional grid (grid hereafter); (b) Fossil fuel fired captive power plant; (c) A carbon intensive mini-grid The baseline scenario would be either continued by use of fossil fuel dominated grid connected electricity generation or fossil fuel used in power plant or carbon intensive electricity.

properties.verra_project_description: The current project activity is implemented by Amalgamated Plantations Private limited (APPL) in its 25 tea estates, located in the diverse agro-ecological regions of two different states, Assam and West Bengal. Common practices in the project area are tea cultivation which include conventional methods such as synthetic fertilizer application, tillage, insecticide application, pesticide application and high-irrigation water consumption. These conventional practices contribute to soil depletion and accelerate GHG emissions. To address these challenges, the project proponent, APPL has ventured into sustainable green initiatives by the production of vermicompost. The construction of vermicompost units and subsequent generation of vermicompost, avoids the production of methane from the agricultural residues and cow dung manure; which would otherwise have been left to decay anaerobically within the project site, and cow dung pits/anaerobic lagoons. The vermicompost produced is then applied to the tea bushes to improve the soil structure and nutrient pool. This is further reflected by quantifying the reduction in emission of greenhouse gases through the project activity, i.e., the production of vermicompost from the wastes. In addition, the vermicompost generated is a powerful soil property enhancer as it is able to transform decomposable material into nutrient-rich organic manure. Hence the project will provide replicable model for environment friendly and economically viable for vermicompost production. During the 10-year crediting period, it is estimated that there will be an average annual reduction and removal of 2,51,964 tCO2e from 2,49,854.39 Metric Tonnes of waste

properties.verra_sectoral_scope_current: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_description: Paddy fields are the most dominant anthropogenic sources of methane in the atmosphere (5-20% of the total emission from all anthropogenic sources). Anaerobic decomposition of organic material in flooded rice fields produces methane, which escapes the atmosphere primarily by transport through the rice plants. The annual CH4 emitted from a given rice area is a function of the number and duration of crops grown, water regimes before and during the cultivation period, and organic and inorganic soil amendments. Soil type, temperature, and rice cultivar also affect CH4 emissions. This CH4 emission-intensive cultivation method will be targeted by the proposed programme, which will involve implementing the technology/measures that result in reduced anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice cropping soils and, thus, reduced methane generation. The project activity comprises of grouped projects of rice fields implementing the following methods: a)	Drum Seeded Rice (DSR) with minimal tillage against transplanted rice cultivation b)	Alternate wetting and Drying Irrigation (AWDI) against conventional flood irrigation in rice

properties.verra_project_description: This complex nexus necessitates the estimation of carbon emissions from groundwater irrigation. Rajan et al. (2020) showed that groundwater irrigation emits 45.3–62.3 MMT of carbon annually (the data seems doubtful; we need to check), contributing 8–11% of India's total carbon emission. This analysis showed that deep tube wells have a huge carbon footprint, and their growing number is a serious environmental concern. Currently, our country accounts for one-fourth of the global groundwater extraction (i.e. 251 km3/year) and uses 90% of the abstracted groundwater for irrigation. Groundwater provides irrigation to around 40–45 million hectares of cultivated land, which is about 60% of the total irrigated area in the Country. Besides stressing the groundwater reserves, intensive groundwater pumping has resulted in higher energy consumption sourced from electricity or fossil fuels, resulting in higher carbon emissions. Judicious and efficient use of water through micro-irrigation can solve the twin problem of accelerated loss of groundwater and reduction of CO2 emissions. Therefore, there is a need to identify practices for efficient water management strategies for different crops and cropping systems and associated GHG emissions. With this background, a project is being proposed with the following specific objectives: i.	To evaluate water and fertilizer savings under micro-irrigation in different agroecological regions of India. ii.	To estimate GHG reduction associated with fertilizer and water saving through micro-irrigation.

properties.verra_project_description: Several horticultural crops are grown in India due to its wide variety of soil and climatic conditions. However, perennial horticultural crops have advantage over annuals as they generally need low inputs such as water, energy, etc., and have high productivity values. Fruit tree-based systems can contribute to carbon sequestration and play an important part in the carbon cycle of terrestrial ecosystems. Because of their propensity to function as carbon sinks and better adaptation to frequent weather aberrations compared with annual crops, fruit tree systems are receiving more attention in recent years and farmers are willing to adopt such systems. Fruit trees such as cashew, mango, guava etc. are reported to have similar carbon sink capacity as forest trees. This capability arises from a variety of factors, including tree lifespan, year-round activity in maintaining living roots, deeper and more widespread root systems; high leaf area index and delayed leaf turnover. Studies from ICCAR-IIHR have indicated that the country as a whole has sequestered 285.005 mt of carbon in its mango orchards. The carbon sequestration potential of different horticultural cropping systems ranked in the order of mango > cashew > rose > vegetable > medicinal and aromatic plants, and addition of more residues in perennial systems to soil records less emission of CO2 than annual crops. As a consequence, perennial horticulture-based systems provide economic gain through carbon credits. Further, enhancement of carbon sequestration in perennial systems can be attained by improving soil health and through better carbon management strategies.

properties.project_name: The potential of plantation-based systems in generating carbon credit through biochar production and application in the West Coast region of India
properties.methodology: VM0044 Methodology for Biochar Utilization in Soil and Non-Soil Applications
properties.project_developer: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development
properties.verra_project_name_current: The potential of plantation-based systems in generating carbon credit through biochar production and application in the West Coast region of India
properties.verra_project_description: The study proposes to prepare biochar from waste material generated in Kulagar (coconut fronds, leaves, coconut and areca nut peelings and husk) using low-cost pyrolysis kilns placed at various locations in these systems. Contributions towards biochar preparation by individual stakeholders (in the biological waste material mode) will be quantified for carbon credits. Biochar (syn. black carbon) acts as a soil conditioner by improving the physical (e.g., bulk density, aggregation, water retention), chemical (e.g., cation exchange capacity), and biochemical (e.g., microbial activity, nutrient recycling) properties of soils, thereby enhancing plant growth. Using biochar as an additional co-benefit in agricultural systems improves soil quality and crop yields and promotes soil carbon sequestration due to its long residence time. Biochar is a recalcitrant material with the inherent capacity to enhance the quality of soil and sequester carbon in the soil. For the pilot study, a number of kulagars covering approximately 25 ha and 20 low-technology biochar conversion units will be taken up in the first phase, potentially converting approximately 17 t/ha/year of plant biomass and subsequently applied back into the soil. The total amount of carbon generated from the biomass and the quantity sequestered in the soil will be determined. Efforts will also be made to use the biochar in non-soil applications, like making briquettes for stoves. The project has a crediting period of 7 years, renewable twice. The first instance of this grouped project is expected to remove an estimated 1061 tCO2e annually and 7427 tCO2e over 7 years.

properties.verra_project_description: The composting project for carbon mitigation is being implemented by M/S ENVRO QUEEN PRIVATE LIMITED. The project involves the installation of numerous compost pits across several villages in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh, India. Its primary objective is to produce organic fertilizer from cow dung, which would otherwise be left to decay at the project site in the absence of such an initiative. This decomposition, if left unmanaged, would result in the emission of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. The project activity includes establishment of aerobic composting pits which entails conversion of animal manure to organic fertilizer through aerobic composting methods by using decomposer. The aerobic treatment of cow dung (which will be collected from farmers of nearby villages) results in avoidance of methane (greenhouse gas) emitted in the pre-project baseline scenario due to anaerobic decomposition of cow dung. Organic compost produced from the composting process are used for application in agricultural activity, is likely to reduce the application of chemical fertilizers and greenhouse gas associated with its productions. Using the manure from the compost pits and by creating working opportunities in local area.

The project covers the geographical boundary of the host country of India. The project aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by encouraging the shift from conventional internal combustion engine vehicles (ICE-V) to electric vehicles, which have a lower carbon footprint, whereby the EV Charging infrastructure results in the avoidance of fossil fuel-powered vehicle usage and resulting in the reduction of the greenhouse gas emissions. properties.verra_project_description: The project activity is a grouped project which includes anaerobic bio digestion systems and biogas units of different capacities. Each project instances will utilize different types of organic waste generated from various source (ex: agriculture field, agro industries, dairy farms & gaushalas, food processing industries, hotels & restaurants etc.). The purpose of this grouped project is to support the development, installation and operation of biogas projects in different locations in India. The technology involved in this project activity is anaerobic digestion technology. The anaerobic decomposition in a continuous stir tank reactor. Anaerobic decomposition is a complex and natural process of degradation of a variety of intermediates into Methane, Carbon-dioxide, and other gases. The project instances will use latest anaerobic Digestion technology to convert biodegradable organic waste into biogas & compressed biogas. The project activities involved in this grouped project manufactures Biogas, Compressed Biogas (CBG) and Biofertilizer using different types of biodegradable wastes. The biowaste digester and Biogas/CBG production system to be installed in each project instances will be of different capacity. The anaerobic digestion is a waste management and renewable energy generation process in which microorganisms break down biodegradable organic waste in the absence of oxygen. Anaerobic digestion technology is considered as the clean & green process to make clean energy and organic content (OC) rich organic manure. to provide clean energy and thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions into the environment.

The biogas plant will use anaerobic digestion technology to convert primarily cow dung and bio-waste into bioCNG. Anaerobic digestion is a waste management and renewable energy generation process in which micro-organisms break down biodegradable organic waste in absence of oxygen. The project activity involves the establishment of biogas plant to generate energy out of primarily cow dung. Project may use other organic waste in small quantity available in nearby areas. Anaerobic digestion is the prominent technology used for degradation of biodegradable organic waste. Anaerobic Digestion (AD) is a biological process that happens naturally when bacteria breaks down organic matter in environments with little or no oxygen. It is effectively a controlled and enclosed version of the anaerobic breakdown of organic waste in disposal site or dumping yard which release methane. The biogas so generated shall be purified further and would be bottled as bio-CNG.

The proposed project activity titled “Mangrove Restoration and Biodiversity Conservation for Coastal communities of India” involves sequestration and storage of carbon (Blue Carbon) through mangrove restoration in degraded coastal land with a focus on coastal community of India. The first instance of the program’s objective is to restore 4,500 ha of degraded coastal area in two years (1st year 2,000 ha; 2nd year 2,500 ha) with native mixed mangrove species plantation in human dominated low-lying landscape of the districts of North & South 24 Parganas and Purba Medinipur (East Midnapore) situated in coastal belt of the state of West Bengal, India. This mangrove restoration project will provide a range of ecosystem services: •	Reduction in GHGs emissions by planting native mixed mangrove species (SDG 13) •	Coastal protection from storm surges, cyclone, sea-level rise and coastal erosions (SDG 14) •	Increased vegetation cover, habitat for wildlife & biodiversity enhancement (SDG 15) •	Water quality regulation through nutrient recycling (SDG 6) •	Supporting fisheries and underwater life (SDG 14) •	Ecotourism and sustainable livelihood (SDG 1, 2 & 8) The project area hosts a population of 44,26,259 spreading over 19 community blocks as per 2011 census out of which ~ 40% falls under Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe category. Population density in this region is 996 per sq km. 38% of its total population are main workers whereas the rest are non-working and marginal working class. Around 15 % of the population of Sundarbans is multidimensionally poor as per Niti Aayog’s latest Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI, 2023). Large-scale community-based mangrove restoration projects can provide long term climate benefit and sustainable livelihood opportunities for these communities.

properties.verra_project_description: The project aims to restore and revitalize 20,000 hectares of degraded agricultural land privately owned by marginal and smallholder farmers, empowering them to adopt diverse, native agroforestry systems. These systems are designed to address both ecological and economic challenges in the region, fostering long-term resilience and sustainability. Key interventions include training farmers in regenerative, climate-resilient agroforestry and agriculture practices tailored to the tropical dryland ecosystem. This involves providing access to high-value saplings of commercial fruit trees, timber species, and non-timber forest products, carefully selected to optimize carbon sequestration and enhance vital ecosystem services such as biodiversity restoration, soil health improvement, and water retention. To combat decades of soil degradation caused by unsustainable monoculture farming, the project will implement advanced soil revitalization techniques. These include the integration of biochar to improve soil fertility, increase organic carbon content, and enhance long-term productivity. Regenerative agricultural practices, such as cover cropping and composting, will also be promoted to restore soil health, increase organic matter, and prevent erosion. Biochar application will complement these efforts by enhancing water retention and nutrient efficiency, critical for this drought-prone region. Beyond ecological restoration, the project aims to uplift the socio-economic well-being of farmers. By diversifying income streams through the production of high-value horticulture crops, and other NTFP products, the project seeks to significantly increase farmers' annual incomes. Additionally, training programs and capacity-building initiatives will equip farmers with the skills and knowledge necessary to adopt and sustain regenerative agroforestry and agriculture practices, creating a replicable model for large-scale landscape restoration.

properties.verra_project_description: The proposed project activity is a Waste to Energy (Bio-CNG) initiative based on a Circular Economy Model, designed to generate approximately 14,000 cubic meters of biogas per day from Municipal Solid Waste (MSW). Through advanced technology and process control mechanisms, it is now highly feasible to convert biodegradable waste—such as MSW, fruit and vegetable waste, and cow dung—into renewable fuels like biogas, Compressed Biogas (CBG) or Bio-CNG, and green electricity, while simultaneously producing valuable by-products including bio-compost and nutrient-rich slurry. The project adopts a proven anaerobic digestion process followed by biogas purification and upgrading to produce Bio-Methane (Bio-CNG). The controlled process parameters ensure optimal gas yield and quality of by-products. These by-products serve as organic fertilizers and soil conditioners, enhancing agricultural productivity and contributing to circular waste management. The initiative promotes environmental sustainability, reduces land and air pollution, supports local livelihoods by generating employment, and provides an alternative source of income for farmers and waste collectors. Prior to the implementation of this project, MSW was openly dumped, leading to unregulated methane emissions—a potent greenhouse gas—thereby contributing significantly to climate change. This project captures methane through controlled anaerobic digestion, purifies and compresses it for sale to Oil Marketing Companies as Bio-CNG, thereby replacing fossil fuels and reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The project has been awarded through a competitive tender process to our company, which met the necessary technical and financial qualifications. The project is currently being implemented at different locations, positioning it as a significant step toward sustainable urban waste management and clean energy transition.

properties.methodology: VM0044 Methodology for Biochar Utilization in Soil and Non-Soil Applications
properties.verra_project_name_current: Carbon Roots - Improving Soil Health with Biochar
properties.verra_project_description: The Carbon Roots Project is a climate resilience and sustainable agriculture initiative aimed at transforming how agricultural waste is managed in rural India. Traditionally, farmers have disposed of crop residues through open burning or by leaving them to decay, both of which release harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere and degrade soil health over time. This project introduces an environmentally responsible alternative by converting agricultural waste biomass into biochar using low-tech, decentralized pyrolysis systems known as TLUD kilns. Trained representatives of the project collect the waste biomass from farmers in nearby areas, process it into biochar on-site, and return the biochar to the farmers mixed with bio fertilizers such as cow manure and compost and applied to the soil. This enhances soil structure, boosts fertility, increases water retention, and sequesters carbon in a stable form within the soil for centuries. The project is being implemented across 10 Indian states and is rooted in principles of regenerative agriculture and circular economy. It not only prevents greenhouse gas emissions from biomass burning and decay but also reduces reliance on chemical fertilizers and supports long-term agricultural productivity. By addressing a major environmental challenge with a locally adaptable and scalable solution, the Carbon Roots Project contributes meaningfully to climate change mitigation and rural development.

Along with the ecological consideration, the species selected was an outcome of consultation with the local communities and stakeholders with an aim to enhance the ecological balance and maximise sustainable livelihoods. The species selection emphasizes biodiversity conservation, incorporating endangered and endemic species into the project. This strategic choice promotes higher tree survival rates and growth, directly contributing to the region's biodiversity and ecological health. Taking cues from a natural forest,  this project includes a multilayer afforestation model that not only optimises land use but also contributes to biodiversity enhancement, thus increasing plantation density to 650 trees per hectare. This project design aids in combating soil erosion, enhances soil fertility, and supports groundwater replenishment in these historically degraded,  barren, and under-utilized lands. Along with enhancing the ecosystem quality of the project area, the project intends to make a significant environmental impact by sequestering an estimated total of 6,377,357 tCO2e during the entire project lifetime.

In addition to increasing carbon stocks, the Project will reduce GHG emissions by preventing land use practices that contribute to emissions - such as soil disturbance from tillage, unmanaged degradation - thereby delivering net climate benefits beyond sequestration alone.

properties.verra_project_name_current: Bio CNG for Sustainable Fuel Solutions project
properties.verra_project_description: The proposed grouped project activity will support the introduction and setting up of Bio-CNG production facilities in India to ensure energy security, fuel mix diversification and sustainable growth of India's fuel retail sector. The main objective of the grouped project is to support the country in establishing field-scale biogas plants by integrating competent biogas technologies and implementation. It is based on the availability of locally resourced feedstock such as agricultural residues, animal manure and other organic wastes. All the Project Activity instances (PAIs) involved in the grouped project includes production of Bio-CNG or Compressed biogas (CBG) as primary product through anaerobic digestion (AD) process. Anaerobic digestion is a key technology for breaking down biodegradable organic waste. This biological process occurs when bacteria decompose organic matter in very low oxygen or in absence of oxygen. Essentially, it’s a controlled version of natural anaerobic breakdown. In this system, organic waste is converted into biogas, a mix of methane and carbon dioxide. Compressed Biogas (CBG) is produced after refining and removing impurities like CO2 and hydrogen sulphide. With methane content exceeding 96%, CBG exceeds industry standards and has properties and calorific value similar to fossil fuel based Compressed Natural Gas (CNG). Economically, project activity provides farmers with an additional revenue stream by allowing them to sell paddy straw/cotton stalk instead of stubble burning. It also generates employment opportunities in paddy straw collection, transportation, and plant operation. Through anaerobic digestion, methane is captured for Bio-CNG production, reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG), promoting cleaner air, and helping combat climate change.

properties.verra_project_description: EverEnviro Resource Management Private Limited  (hereafter referred to as EERMPL) is developing a Grouped Project aimed at producing renewable Bio-CNG from organic waste, with multiple plant locations across India. The goal of this initiative is to reduce methane emissions from unmanaged waste like biomass residue and animal manure by processing it through anaerobic digestion, and to supply purified Bio-CNG for use in the transport sector. This grouped project allows the inclusion of multiple project proponents operating individual Bio-CNG plants at various locations across India, all following a common technology and methodology framework. Before these plants were operational, the organic waste — especially biomass residue and animal manure — was largely unmanaged. It was typically dumped by farmers in pits to make digestate until it becomes suitable to be used as fertiliser,  and left to decay/ burned in cases of paddy straw. Similarly, cow dung was either disposed of informally or left to decompose in open fields. Both these practices contributed to uncontrolled methane emissions. There was no system in place to capture and use the methane generated from this decay. With the project now operational, methane that would have been released into the atmosphere is captured through sealed anaerobic digesters and directed to an upgrading system that produces high-purity methane. This methane is compressed into Bio-CNG and supplied to customers in the transport sector. For the initial four project activity instances, the projected average annual  GHG emission reductions are estimated at 189,582 tCO₂e, with a cumulative reduction of approximately 1,327,078 tCO₂e over the first seven-year crediting period.

properties.verra_project_description: The proposed project activity is being implemented by Rama Greens, a partnership firm located in Haryana, India. The project aims to establish a Bio-CNG production facility based on anaerobic digestion of organic waste materials such as press mud, poultry litter, and cattle dung. The facility is designed to process approximately 165 metric tons per day (TPD) of these organic waste streams to generate about 15,000 m3 per day of raw biogas. The biogas will then be upgraded to produce 6,000 kg/day of high-quality Bio-CNG using Pressure Swing Adsorption (PSA) technology. Additionally, the project will generate approximately 40 TPD of solid manure and 160 kiloliters/day of liquid digestate as by-products, which will be utilized as bio-fertilizers. A key feature of this project is that the produced Bio-CNG will be injected into the existing natural gas pipeline infrastructure operated by entities such as GAIL or IGL, for subsequent distribution and use in domestic households. This approach enables the substitution of LPG (Liquified  Petroleum Gas) with a renewable, low-carbon alternative in household cooking and heating applications. In the absence of the project, the baseline scenario would involve the unmanaged decay of organic waste, leading to methane emissions, and continued reliance on LPG as fuel for cooking in households. By establishing a controlled anaerobic digestion system and displacing fossil fuel use in domestic energy applications, the project results in significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. These emission reductions will be monitored and verified as per the methodologies listed and are eligible to generate Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) under the VCS Program. The project was commissioned on 20 January 2024. Based on current projections, the project is expected to achieve a total emission reduction of approximately 395,145 tCO₂e over a 7-year crediting period, with an average annual emission reduction of 56,449 tCO₂e

properties.methodology: VM0044 Methodology for Biochar Utilization in Soil and Non-Soil Applications
properties.verra_project_name_current: PrithviPoshan Biochar Project
properties.verra_project_description: The PrithviPoshan Biochar Project is a large-scale carbon sequestration initiative focused on converting cow dung into biochar to address rising greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improve agricultural sustainability. The feedstock is sourced from a partner organization Shri Godham Mahateerth Pathmeda Lok Punyarth Nyas, a Non-Governmental Organization that operates a network of cow shelters (gaushalas) with over 150,000 cattle. The project utilizes a high-tech pyrolysis facility capable of processing 100 tonnes of manure daily to produce approximately 14,600 dry metric tonnes of biochar annually. The system is a continuous rotary system where pyrolysis gases are scrubbed and utilized to heat the pyrolytic chamber and the excess gas combusted in a thermal oxidizer with waste heat recovery, thus avoiding methane emissions. Excess heat from the thermal oxidizer is utilized to dry and preheat the feedstock before it enters the pyrolysis chamber. The feedstock will be pyrolyzed at an optimized temperature of 550℃, which exceeds the World Biochar Certificate (WBC) requirement of 500℃ for 3 minutes for animal manure, ensuring the elimination of biological hazards and micropollutants. Automated metering and an IOT-enabled interface are used to log production parameters such as feedstock input, biochar output, and pyrolysis chamber temperature, ensuring tamper-proof data for verification. The produced biochar undergoes rigorous quality assurance, with samples tested for moisture, organic carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) to ensure permanence and compliance with standards like a molar H/Corg ratio less than 0.7. This is a grouped project with facilities located in India. The first project activity /instance (the Nandgaon facility) is located in the Vadvaj Village, District Sirohi, Rajasthan. The biochar plant is strategically located within the premises of the Shree Manorama Golok Teerth - Nandgaon gaushala (source of waste generation) to minimize transport-related emissions. The project will use bullock carts to transport waste from various pens within the gaushala to the production facility. The primary mechanism is the conversion of waste cow manure into biochar, a stable form of carbon. This process directly reduces methane emissions that would otherwise be released from decomposing manure. The biochar produced is a long-term carbon sink, enhancing soil health and providing carbon sequestration benefits when applied to agricultural land. The project specifically ensures non-combustive use of biochar as a soil amendment. The Nandgaon facility alone is estimated to remove 18,415 tCO2e of GHG emissions from the atmosphere annually for a total of 1,28,908 tCO2e over the first crediting period i.e. 1 July 2026 to 30th June 2033.

properties.project_name: AgriCapture South Asia Rice Methane Project
properties.methodology: VM0051 Improved Management in Rice Production Systems
properties.project_type: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_primary_category: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_name_current: AgriCapture South Asia Rice Methane Project
properties.verra_sectoral_scope_current: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_description: The AgriCapture South Asia Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in South Asia in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation. Continuous flooding creates an anaerobic soil environment that fosters methane producing microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). Methane emissions rise as the duration of the flooded period increases, due to the buildup of these microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). By introducing periods of drying that allow oxygen to reenter the soil, improved irrigation practices, like single-drainage and alternate wetting and drying (AWD), can significantly reduce methane emissions. Research indicates that AWD lowers methane emissions by 47% while also decreasing water consumption by up to 39% (Gao, 2024; Atwill R. L., 2020). Participating growers may also transition from transplanted rice to direct seeded rice, another improved irrigation practice. Traditional transplanted rice involves rice seedlings being grown in a nursery before being planted in puddled fields (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). The process requires a prohibitive amount of labor, and puddling the field requires large amounts of irrigation (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). Additionally, the puddled fields established before planting increases methane emissions due to increasing the period of anaerobic conditions (Reddy, et al., 2025). When compared to transplanted rice, direct seeded rice reduces methane emissions and water consumption by 70% and 8-12% respectively (Reddy, et al., 2025; Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020).

properties.verra_project_description: This project, located in Bangalore, Karnataka, India, implements an innovative waste management solution using Black Soldier Fly (BSF) larvae-based aerobic composting technology. The facility processes 300 metric tons per day (TPD) of organic municipal solid waste (wet fraction only), diverting it from landfills to a controlled biological treatment system. BSF larvae (Hermetia illucens) accelerate the decomposition of organic matter under optimized aerobic conditions, producing nutrient-rich compost for agricultural use and larvae biomass for animal feed—supporting circular economy principles. The system ensures efficient stabilization of organic matter while preventing anaerobic conditions, thereby minimizing methane emissions. By replacing conventional landfill disposal, the project avoids methane (CH₄) emissions—a greenhouse gas with a Global Warming Potential (GWP) 28 times that of CO₂. Emission reductions are quantified using the CDM methodology ACM0022: Alternative Waste Treatment Processes (Version 03.0) under the VCS Standard. Prior to implementation, organic MSW was disposed of in unmanaged landfills without methane capture, resulting in significant GHG emissions. The project introduces a sustainable alternative aligned with climate mitigation and resource recovery goals. The proposed activity is expected to generate an average annual GHG emission reduction of approximately 58,940 tCO₂e, with a total of about 589,401 tCO₂e over a 10-year fixed crediting period. The project is designed as a grouped project, and this is the first project activity instance (PAI#01) under the group. Additional project activities will be added in the future after validation, enabling scalability and broader impact. Mukka Protein Limited serves as the project proponent and developer, responsible for implementation, management, and monitoring.

The project is expected to benefit more than 134,000 marginal farmers and generate around 15,000 person-days of employment annually. Aligned with India’s Nationally Determined Contributions, the project contributes to the national target of creating an additional carbon sink of 56,787,786 tCO₂e by 2052, while demonstrating a replicable, nature-based solution for climate mitigation, adaptation, and sustainable livelihoods in Telangana.

properties.project_name: Biogas to power and heat generation project by SKM Egg Products Export India Limited
properties.methodology: AMS-I.F. Renewable electricity generation for captive use and mini-grid; AMS-III.D. Methane recovery in animal manure management systems
properties.verra_project_name_current: Biogas to power and heat generation project by SKM Egg Products Export India Limited
properties.verra_project_description: The project employs a controlled anaerobic digestion system consisting of feedstock preprocessing, slurry homogenization, digestion, biogas purification, power generation, and digestate management. The primary raw materials are poultry litter (70 tonnes per day) and cow dung (5 tonnes per day). These materials are collected from the poultry and cow farm and delivered to two unloading platforms, ensuring continuous and balanced feeding of the system. The prepared slurry is pumped into two anaerobic digesters, each with a capacity of approximately 6,832 m³. Inside the digesters, the slurry undergoes biomethanation under anaerobic and mesophilic conditions, where organic matter is biologically decomposed into biogas and digestate. The digestion process occurs over a controlled hydraulic retention time to ensure stable methane production. Biogas generated in the digesters is collected and routed to a raw biogas balloon, with a total production of approximately 7,000 m³ of biogas per day. The raw biogas primarily consists of methane (50–60%) and carbon dioxide (40–45%), with trace amounts of oxygen and hydrogen sulfide. The cleaned biogas is utilized in two ways: Approximately 20% of the biogas is fed into biogas engine-generator sets to produce renewable electricity, generating around 1,680 kWh per day. The remaining 80% of biogas is supplied to biogas burners or boilers for thermal applications.

properties.verra_project_description: Rice cultivation in continuously flooded paddy fields, as currently practiced in the project area, is one of the dominant anthropogenic sources of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly methane (CH4) emissions. As rice in India is cultivated primarily by smallholder farmers, it is crucial to address these GHG emissions in a multi-stakeholder program with on-the-ground support. Activities and technologies to reduce GHG emissions must be readily available and implementable for smallholders, considering water shortage and potential soil fertility issues as well as labor constraints in these farming systems. The objective of The Good Rice Alliance improved rice production program in India is to address the methane-intensive method of flooded rice cultivation to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by introducing various agricultural practices that contribute to reducing the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter. The project focuses on transitioning rice farms from the conventional method of continuous flooding to the alternating wetting and drying (AWD) technique. AWD introduces controlled irrigation with periodical flooding and monitoring of the water table to ensure soil aeriation while maintaining optimal water supply to ensure full rice yield. In its initial phase, TGRA involves more than 12,000 smallholder farmers who cultivate more than 16,000 hectares of rice fields with one or two rice growing seasons per year. The program is implemented in collaboration with regional partners in all participating states. The program improves the farmers’ livelihoods by reducing their production costs and improving yield, supported by direct payments for participating in the project. Production efficiency gain, yield increase and water savings provide multiple SDG benefits beyond SDG 13, namely contributions to SDG 2 and SDG 6. The estimated net GHG emission reductions from the project are 181,500 tCO2 equivalent per year, over a crediting period of 10 years.

At its core, the initiative integrates Improved Crop Management (ICM) with agroforestry systems to transition conventional farming into resilient, low-emission production systems. Farmers are supported through targeted capacity building and guidance on fair and stable pricing mechanisms. Over the project lifetime, the program is conservatively estimated to generate approximately 13,510,674 tCO₂e in verified emission reductions and removals, corresponding to an average annual net removal of approximately 337,767 tCO₂e. Beyond carbon benefits, the initiative delivers significant co-benefits, including improved soil health, enhanced water retention, increased climate resilience, and diversified farmer incomes through both productivity gains and carbon finance. Positioned as a scalable natural climate solution, HIM Evergreen presents a compelling opportunity for investors seeking measurable climate impact alongside long-term environmental and socio-economic value.

Purpose: The project aims to recover methane-rich biogas produced during the anaerobic treatment of wastewater. The recovered biogas is currently being utilized for in-house electricity generation. The generated biogas is used as a renewable fuel in the plant's boiler, replacing some portion of fossil fuel which is coal. In the event of a temporary shutdown of the biogas plant unit, any surplus methane will be safely combusted through a controlled open flare system to prevent its release into the atmosphere. Future Prospects: In upcoming days Sillverton Industries Limited are planning to compressed the biogas generated will then be upgraded to Bio-CNG and utilized as a clean transport fuel, thereby replacing fossil-based alternatives and mitigating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Through this biological conversion, the project is expected to generate around 9TPD or 9091  m³/day of raw biogas, with methane concentration exceeding 55%. The biogas will be purified using a Pressure Swing Adsorption (PSA) system to produce Bio-Compressed Natural Gas (Bio-CNG). This high-purity Bio-CNG will be bottled or injected into the distribution network and supplied for use in transportation applications, replacing conventional fuels such Fossil fuel CNG thereby contributing directly to the decarbonization of the transport sector. By capturing methane from wastewater and upgrading it for productive use, the project prevents its uncontrolled release

properties.verra_project_description: The proposed project is an Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) project under the category of Afforestation, Reforestation and Revegetation (ARR) of the VCS standard. The project is designed as a grouped project. This first project activity instance (PAI1) comprises up to 8,000,000 trees across Khandwa district of the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh in an area approximately 40,000 hectare. The objective of the project is to increase the tree cover outside forest areas through ARR activities on privately owned lands of local farmers. Based on the available space and the farmer’s preferences, planting will primarily be done along bunds, with the option of block plantations where suitable. These could include fallow lands or lands with sparse vegetation. The species, planting design, and planting density are determined jointly by the farmer and the project team and depend on suitability of species and design as well as farmer preferences and available land. The project ensures that no native ecosystems were cleared in the ten years prior to project start and that there is no ecosystem change, or net harm, because of project implementation. The project aims to secure the financial security of the local farming and other communities through planting of farmer friendly trees to support traditional crop-based agriculture systems. The project team on the ground are employed from the local community, and care is taken to ensure participation of women and other marginalized members of the community. The planting activities occur on predominantly privately owned agricultural lands and consist of planting farmer friendly trees. These could include timber, fruit, fodder, medicinal and forest trees. All species are native or naturalized, and none of the species are invasive or known to have adverse impacts on local ecology.

properties.verra_project_description: The project activity involves the installation and operation of a poultry litter-based biogas-to-power generation facility by SKM Animal Feeds and Foods (India) Pvt. Ltd. at its poultry farm located in Village Koduvilarpatti, Theni District, Tamil Nadu, India. The facility utilizes approximately 20 tonnes of poultry litter per day generated from around 150,000 birds maintained at the farm. The project reduces greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions through two mechanisms. First, the controlled anaerobic digestion process captures methane that would otherwise be released into the atmosphere from unmanaged decomposition of poultry litter. Second, the renewable electricity generated from biogas displaces electricity that would otherwise be sourced from the fossil fuel-dominated grid, thereby avoiding associated CO₂ emissions. Additionally, the production of organic manure reduces dependence on synthetic fertilizers.

properties.verra_sectoral_scope_current: Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use
properties.verra_project_description: This project is an Afforestation, Reforestation and Revegetation (ARR) activity implemented in Ri Bhoi District, Meghalaya, India, under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) using the VCS-approved methodology VM0047 v1.1. The project aims to restore degraded and fallow lands through the plantation of native bamboo species Bambusa tulda across approximately 100 hectares in the initial phase, with potential for expansion through additional Project Activity Instances (PAIs). The targeted lands were historically used for agriculture but have lost fertility due to unsustainable cultivation practices. The plantation model restores ecological function by improving soil structure, enhancing moisture retention, and increasing vegetation cover, thereby contributing to biodiversity enhancement and long-term land productivity. Carbon removals are quantified through improved biomass and carbon stocks in line with VM0047 v1.1 requirements. Participating households contribute land and labor and benefit through employment in nursery development, plantation, maintenance, and bamboo harvesting activities, as well as a share in revenues from bamboo utilization and carbon credits. The project prioritizes inclusive development, ensuring active participation of women and marginalized communities.
